title: Moonlit Night on the Dnieper
source: State Russian Museum, St Petersburg (public domain). Oil on canvas, 105 x 144 cm. Full resolution from Wikimedia Commons: File:0857Ha. Куинджи А.И. Лунная ночь на Днепре.jpg (4067 x 2955 px)
caption: In 1880, St Petersburg queued down the street to see just one painting. Some visitors even looked behind it. #moonlight #nightsky #kuindzhi #fineart #artfacts
_verify: VERIFIED, Wikipedia EN (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonlit_Night_on_the_Dnieper): 1880, oil on canvas, 105 x 144 cm, Russian Museum; Grand Duke Konstantin Konstantinovich bought it from the studio before it was exhibited; shown alone in the hall of the Society for the Encouragement of Artists, St Petersburg; curtains lowered, artificial light on the painting; long queue, visitors admitted in groups; 'some accounts say' visitors believed a lamp lit it from behind and searched for the light source.

VERIFIED, Izvestia (iz.ru/796997/sergei-uvarov/put-v-nochi-drama-arkhipa-kuindzhi-i-ego-glavnogo-shedevra): exhibition on Bolshaya Morskaya 38, dark hall, only a beam of electric light on the canvas; the queue reached almost to Nevsky Prospect; viewers looked behind the canvas for a lamp; the Grand Duke bought it unfinished (Kuindzhi: 'about five thousand'); loaded on the ship 'Duke of Edinburgh' in Sept 1880 and travelled with him until Jan 1882; Turgenev feared it would come back ruined by the salty sea air; the first version has darkened.

VERIFIED with nuance, bitumen: 360.ru (360.ru/tekst/obschestvo/volshebnyj-svet-i-bitum/): Kuindzhi experimented with pigments and actively used bitumen, which decomposes and darkens under light and air; the painting's paints changed irreversibly and darkened. The article does not prove bitumen is THE cause for this canvas; slide 8 says he experimented with pigments including bitumen, which darkens with age, and that the painting is darker today.

CAUTIOUS: 'looking behind the canvas for a lamp' is told as an anecdote (Wikipedia: 'some accounts say'); slide 5 says 'Accounts say'. Slide 3 says 'a single beam of light' (Izvestia: electric light; Wikipedia: artificial light).
INTERPRETATION, slide 6: that the dark bank and huts make the moonlight seem brighter is a visual reading of contrast, not a sourced quote.

UNVERIFIED, not used: exact exhibition dates, waiting times in hours, Mendeleev's role beyond visiting the studio (Wikipedia lists him among studio visitors), Kuindzhi's later withdrawal from exhibiting.
Focus boxes estimated from the contact sheet thumbnail; re-tune on the real image.

slides.headline: A whole city queued for one painting
slides.sub: Arkhip Kuindzhi, Moonlit Night on the Dnieper, 1880

slides.headline: St Petersburg, 1880
slides.text: St Petersburg, 1880. Arkhip Kuindzhi shows just one painting, a simple landscape, alone in a hall. Yet the queue stretches down the street.

slides.headline: A dark room
slides.text: Inside, the curtains are drawn. The room is dark, and a single beam of light falls on the canvas. Visitors enter in small groups.

slides.headline: The moon
slides.text: Out of the blackness, a greenish moon breaks through the clouds. It doesn't look painted. It looks switched on.

slides.headline: Light on the water
slides.text: Below, its light spills across the Dnieper. Accounts say some visitors were so baffled they checked behind the canvas for a hidden lamp.

slides.headline: No lamp, just paint
slides.text: There was no lamp. Only paint: Kuindzhi kept the riverbank and its little huts nearly black, so the moonlight seems to burn.

slides.headline: A Grand Duke's voyage
slides.text: But Grand Duke Konstantin Konstantinovich had already bought it, even before the show. Then he took it on a long sea voyage.

slides.headline: Fading light
slides.text: Turgenev feared the salty air would ruin it. And Kuindzhi experimented with pigments, including bitumen, which darkens with age. Today it's much darker.

slides.headline: A shadow of 1880
slides.text: What we see now is only a shadow of what those crowds saw. Be honest: would you have looked behind the canvas too?
